title: Coulomb's Levitator
summary: Give a small ball just the right charge for the repulsion from a fixed charge to hold it floating at a marked height.
subject: physics
learningOutcome: After winning, the student can balance Coulomb's force against weight, solve for the charge from the height, handle small-scale units, and use signs to tell repulsion from attraction.

levels.title: Raise the ball
levels.adds: Baseline: give the ball a charge so it floats at the marked height. The height is shown, so you can experiment.
hints: The ball hangs where the electric force pushing it up exactly equals its weight pulling it down.
Coulomb's force falls with the square of the distance, so more charge lifts the ball higher, but not in proportion.
Compare two tries: doubling the charge multiplies the height by about 1.41. So height squared is proportional to the charge.

levels.title: Work it out
levels.adds: New idea: there is no height readout. Calculate the charge from the balance k q Q / h² = m g before you release the ball.
hints: Write the balance: electric force = weight, so k q Q / h² = m g.
Solve for q: q = m g h² / (k Q). Convert grams, centimetres and microcoulombs to kg, m and C first.
Use g = 9.8 m/s² and k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².

levels.title: Tiny scale
levels.adds: Harder: milligrams, millimetres and nanocoulombs. The answer is a charge in picocoulombs.
hints: Convert first: 1 mg = 10⁻⁶ kg, 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 nC = 10⁻⁹ C.
The balance is the same: q = m g h² / (k Q).
1 pC = 10⁻¹² C, so a charge of 6.8 × 10⁻¹¹ C is 68 pC.

levels.title: Opposite base
levels.adds: New idea: the base may be negative. A ball with the opposite sign is attracted and falls, so choose the right sign as well as the right size.
hints: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. To float, the ball must be repelled.
Look at the sign of the base charge and give the ball the same sign.
Then find the size exactly as before: q = m g h² / (k Q), using the sizes (magnitudes) of the charges.

misconceptions: Doubling the charge doubles the hover height
Forgetting to convert prefixes (mg, mm, nC) to SI units
A ball with the opposite charge can still float
